prompt: This is one actual native Vulkan capture of a triangulated surface with a fixed boundary, viewed horizontally through its boundary plane. Describe only visible geometry and silhouette. What, if anything, shows the center relative to the boundary? Identify ambiguity and visibility defects. Do not infer numerical heights, forces, physical time, simulation correctness or human acceptance. Previous oblique views were inconclusive; that is context, not an expected answer.
raw_response:
**Visible geometry and silhouette (literal, no inference)**

The frame is divided by a sharp horizontal color discontinuity at mid‑height: pure black above, uniform dark gray below. In the lower half sits a centered, darker hexagon with flat top/bottom edges and pointy left/right vertices; its top edge lies on that horizontal line, and its leftmost/rightmost corners give it the widest horizontal extent. Above the line there is exactly one geometric feature: a thin, very low, light‑gray triangular sliver ("tent") whose base rests on the line and whose apex sits at horizontal center. The two tips of this sliver reach out to roughly the hexagon's extreme left/right points (i.e. wider than the hexagon's top edge). Its fill is a smooth gradient, brightest at the apex and darkening toward the base. Inside the sliver are a few faint interior edges radiating from the apex down to points on the base (a fan‑like pattern), rendered at low contrast against that gradient. Nothing else rises above the line; there is no separate bright wireframe outlining the boundary above it — the in‑plane extent of the boundary is only implied by the sliver's base and by the hexagon below.

**What shows the center relative to the boundary**

Only the thin raised silhouette — the shallow peak above the horizontal line, with its apex at the center — indicates that the central region lies out of the boundary plane on the upper side. Because the camera looks edge‑on through that plane, this is seen as a 1‑D profile (the top contour plus the faint fan edges), not as any visible face area of the bump; the brighter shading at the apex is lighting, not geometry. Everything that lies *in* the plane (the flat membrane / boundary ring) collapses onto the line and contributes no visible area, so the center is distinguished from the boundary solely by this nonzero protrusion above the line.

**Ambiguities and visibility defects**

- *In‑plane shape invisible.* The boundary polygon's true 2‑D shape and any flat region project to a single horizontal line, so they carry no visible extent. The dark hexagon below the line is ambiguous: it could be the back side of the surface, a projection/shadow, or an unrelated background element; its vertical relationship to the surface cannot be determined from this view.
- *Sign / occlusion.* Only material that pokes above the plane appears as the sliver. Any downward component would fall into the gray region and merge with the hexagon/background, so it is not possible to confirm whether the central feature is purely upward or straddles the plane. Its off‑plane magnitude is also not visible — only that it is nonzero.
- *Topology partly hidden.* The interior fan edges are low contrast; several expected center‑to‑boundary edges do not appear as distinct lines (coincident in projection or masked by the gradient), so the exact triangulation/topology cannot be read off this view.
- *Boundary vertex ordering indistinguishable.* All boundary vertices project onto the same horizontal line, so no relative height among them is visible — they are merely collinear points on the line.
- *Symmetry not confirmable.* The left/right silhouette looks mirror‑symmetric, but the low‑contrast internal edges prevent confirming or denying asymmetry.
- *No explicit boundary outline above the line.* The horizontal color split spans the whole frame (wider than the object), so it reads as a background/ground plane rather than a drawn boundary wireframe; consequently the "boundary" itself has no visible edge above the line — only the sliver's base marks where geometry meets it.

In short, this horizontal‑through‑the‑plane view reduces the surface to a thin top profile plus an ambiguous dark hexagon below; it reveals that the center protrudes out of the plane but discards all in‑plane shape, height ordering, and most interior topology.
